canonical_answers.title: Report — Repeated Exhaust-Valve Failures on Medium-Speed Auxiliary Engines
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**Report to the Superintendent Engineer regarding a number of cases of severe damage to medium-speed engine exhaust valves in the previous 12 months, outlining probable cause and future steps to avoid similar incidents (16)**

**1. Introduction**: submitted following a number of severe exhaust-valve-related failures on auxiliary-engine units #1, #2, #4 and #6 during the past twelve months, to record the sequence of incidents, identify probable root causes, and recommend corrective measures — based on engine-room log entries, alarm records, overhaul reports and the onboard spare-gear inventory.

**2. Summary of incidents**:
- **Case 1 — Unit #4**: black smoke at the engine block activated the water-mist system; the engine was stopped and inspected. A broken exhaust-valve spring allowed the spindle to free-fall onto the piston crown, shattering the cylinder head and spindle and damaging the valve guide, with exhaust gas released into the engine room. The complete cylinder-head assembly was renewed with an overhauled spare.
- **Case 2 — Unit #1**: a knocking noise was detected; inspection identified excessive tappet clearance. The engine was stopped and clearance reset per the manufacturer's manual — no catastrophic damage, but incorrect valve setting accelerates seat wear and imposes impact stress on valve components.
- **Case 3 — Unit #6**: high exhaust gas temperature was recorded; inspection found a broken valve spindle leaking gas into the manifold. Owing to a shortage of new spindles, used spindles had been repeatedly lapped and reused; material fatigue and thermal stress on the aged component caused the failure. The cylinder-head assembly was renewed with an overhauled spare.
- **Case 4 — Unit #6 (a second incident)**: during routine tappet/timing adjustment the exhaust valve was found stuck in its guide. Dismantling revealed heavy carbon on the spindle, traced to an incorrectly "clocked" lube-oil drive line that formed an oil trap and contamination build-up. The head was decarbonised, the spindle bore cleaned, leak-tested and returned to service.
- **Pattern**: the failures share common threads — broken/aged valve components, incorrect clearances, deposit build-up and elevated exhaust temperatures — indicating a systemic cause (spares and maintenance management, plus operational loading) rather than isolated component defects.

**3. Probable causes**: inadequate critical-spare availability (insufficient stock of cylinder heads, spindles, springs and valve gear, delaying full renewals); repeated reuse of aged components (spindles repeatedly lapped and reused, reducing material strength and causing fatigue failure); incorrect valve setting (excessive tappet clearance causing impact loading and accelerated wear); improper lubrication-line configuration (mis-aligned oil drive line creating an oil trap, carbon accumulation and valve sticking); operational overloading (engines run under sustained overload, particularly while other units were under maintenance, raising thermal/mechanical stress — with high-temperature vanadium/sodium hot corrosion and cat-fines ruled out via fuel analysis). Collectively these indicate a combination of mechanical fatigue, thermal overloading, poor spare management and maintenance constraints.

**4. Recommendations** (linked to each cause above): procure and hold adequate onboard stock of genuine, manufacturer-approved critical spares (spindles, springs, guides, complete cylinder-head assemblies) and stop reusing over-lapped spindles; carry out a comprehensive major overhaul of the affected engines at the next dry dock, renewing all critical valve-train components; enforce PMS tappet-clearance and timing checks, verify valve-rotator operation, and correct the lube-oil drive-line alignment to prevent oil traps and carbon build-up; avoid sustained overload, verifying AVR/PMS load-sharing and governor balancing so load is shared smoothly; trend individual exhaust-gas temperatures, vibration and tappet clearances, arranging shore-specialist vibration/fatigue analysis to catch component stress early; improve maintenance planning and shore coordination so spares arrive and maintenance windows are honoured despite the operating schedule.

**5. Conclusion**: the repeated failures are primarily attributable to material fatigue, insufficient spare support, operational overloading and maintenance constraints; without a structured corrective plan, recurrence is likely and may lead to major engine breakdown and extended off-hire.
examiner_focus: The question required a Report but, as usual, a large portion of candidates just wrote an essay. There was also a lack of structure and continuity in answers which often drifted from topic to topic in a random manner — marks come from report format and structure (heading block, decimal-numbered headed sections in a logical order, each recommendation linked back to its cause) as much as from the engineering content.

canonical_answers.title: Diesel Generator — Preparing & Selecting as Standby, and Post-Shutdown Checking Procedure
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) How a diesel generator is prepared and selected as a standby generator (8)**

This assumes the engine is already mechanically fit (that is part b). The task here is to bring it to a state of armed readiness and select it at the board.

1. Confirm auxiliaries and pre-start state — sump oil level correct, jacket water level up and the jacket-water pre-heater ON (kept warm so it can accept load immediately), fuel service/day-tank level good and fuel valves open, starting-air receiver at pressure (or start batteries charged), governor set.
2. Keep-warm/pre-lubrication running — the standby set is held warm (heater) and, where fitted, the pre-lube/priming pump runs continuously or cyclically so there is an oil film on start, avoiding thermal and lubrication shock when it auto-starts onto load.
3. Test run — start the engine locally, warm it through and run at no load; check lube-oil pressure, cooling-water and exhaust temperatures, governor stability and that it reaches rated speed with no abnormal noise/leaks; then stop (or leave running to synchronise).
4. Prove the electrical end — confirm the AVR builds rated voltage at correct frequency, and that phase sequence/rotation is correct for paralleling.
5. Set up the breaker and controls — ACB racked into the service (connected) position, control/tripping fuses in, undervoltage relay healthy, synchronising unit set to auto.
6. Select to STANDBY/AUTO on the PMS or selector switch — arm the set so it will auto-start on demand (blackout, load-dependent start, or a heavy-consumer request), and set its start priority/sequence in the load-sharing order.
7. Confirm standby readiness — with keep-warm and pre-lube running, starting air/batteries topped up, the set is now able to start, synchronise and be on the bars within ~45 seconds, sharing kW (governors) and kVAr (AVR) automatically.

**(b) Procedure for checking a diesel generator engine after shutdown, before it is returned to standby duty (8)**

This is the physical engine round after it has been running or worked on, worked through methodically:

1. Make safe/tidy up — engine correctly stopped; if maintenance was carried out, confirm all tools and rags accounted for, guards and covers refitted, and any isolation removed.
2. Lubricating oil — check sump level and top up; check oil condition (no water/fuel contamination, correct colour/smell); check LO filter differential pressure and clean/change if due; sample if scheduled.
3. Cooling water — check jacket/expansion-tank level and top up with treated water; verify inhibitor/treatment concentration; check the header tank and confirm no leaks.
4. Fuel oil — check service/day-tank level, drain off any water, check/clean filters, confirm no leaks, and prime/vent the system so it is ready to fire.
5. Starting system — top up and drain the starting-air receiver of water/oil (or check battery charge and electrolyte); confirm air-start valves and pressure are correct.
6. Bar over/check for hydraulic lock — open the indicator (test) cocks, engage turning gear and bar the engine over one revolution (or blow through on air) to prove free rotation and that no water/oil has collected in a cylinder; then disengage turning gear and close the cocks.
7. Leak and integrity check — walk round for oil, water, fuel, air and exhaust leaks; check the turbocharger, and drain any water from the charge-air cooler.
8. Governor and linkages — check governor oil level and that the fuel-rack/control linkages move freely.
9. Protection and alarms — confirm trips and alarms are reset and healthy (LO low-pressure, HT high-temperature, overspeed), and instrumentation reads correctly.
10. Replenish and warm through — with all consumables topped up, pre-heater on and pre-lube running, the engine is now physically fit — then it can be prepared and selected to standby per part (a).
examiner_focus: Some candidates confused part (a) and part (b), or wrote the same content in both. Keep the two halves separate: part (a) is operational/electrical — running the set up, keeping it warm and arming it at the switchboard/PMS so it auto-starts and shares load on demand; part (b) is a mechanical post-shutdown checklist — the hands-on round after the engine has run, to prove it is physically fit.

canonical_answers.title: Engine Cooling-Water Waste Heat Recovery — Electricity Generation (Organic Rankine Cycle) & Ship Heating Utilisation
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**(a) Engine cooling-water waste heat recovery system for generating electricity, with a sketch, explaining how it operates (8)**

**[Sketch]** Organic Rankine Cycle recovering jacket cooling-water heat to generate electricity: evaporator → expander/generator → seawater condenser → feed pump, a closed loop.

The engine's jacket cooling water (~80–90°C) is the heat source. Because that temperature is far too low to boil water usefully, the system uses a closed Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) charged with a low-boiling-point organic fluid — a refrigerant such as R245fa or R134a, or a hydrocarbon like isopentane.

How it operates (a closed loop, like a fridge run as a heat engine):

1. **Evaporator** — the hot jacket water gives up its heat to the organic fluid, boiling it into a high-pressure vapour (the jacket water leaves cooler and returns to the engine/central cooler).
2. **Expander/turbine** — the high-pressure vapour expands through a turbine or screw expander, doing shaft work that drives a coupled generator/alternator, producing electricity fed to the main switchboard (through a converter/synchronising gear).
3. **Condenser** — the low-pressure exhaust vapour is cooled by seawater (or the central fresh-water cooler) and condensed back to liquid.
4. **Feed pump** — pumps the liquid back up to evaporator pressure, completing the cycle.

This recovers low-grade heat that would otherwise be dumped to sea, cutting diesel-generator load, fuel consumption and CO₂/EEDI. The ORC can be combined with scavenge-air and lube-oil cooler heat, or topped up by an exhaust-gas source, to boost output.

**(b) How waste heat recovered from diesel engine cooling water is utilised throughout the ship for different heating purposes, and how such systems are operated (8)**

**[Sketch]** Utilisation of recovered jacket cooling-water heat: a three-way control valve feeds the fresh-water generator, HVAC/accommodation, domestic hot water and oil heating, with surplus dumped through the central cooler.

The jacket water leaving the engine carries a large quantity of low-grade heat that would otherwise be rejected to sea. Dedicated heat exchangers tap this circuit; a three-way temperature-control valve gives the heating services first call on the heat, with the seawater central cooler removing only the surplus, so the jacket stays at its ~85°C set-point. Main uses:

- **Fresh-water (distilling) plant** — the biggest and classic use. Jacket water heats a vacuum evaporator: under vacuum, seawater boils at only ~40–60°C, so 80–85°C jacket water is hot enough to distil it. Vapour is condensed to distilled water; a salinometer dumps any off-spec water. Only run at sea, clear of the coast.
- **HVAC/accommodation heating** — jacket water (or a secondary hot-water loop it heats via an exchanger) feeds the air-heater batteries in the ventilation/AC plant and cabin heaters.
- **Domestic hot water** — heats a calorifier supplying washrooms and galley.
- **Fuel-oil and lube-oil tank heating** — base/tank-maintenance heating of HFO settling and service tanks to keep viscosity and pumpability (final heating to injection viscosity still needs steam or electric heaters).

Operating philosophy: temperature-controlled and load-dependent — recovery services are prioritised and the central cooler dumps the balance. At low engine load, or in port, there may be too little heat, so a steam or electric heater (auxiliary/composite boiler) backs up the services. The cooled jacket water returns to the engine, keeping cylinder-liner temperatures stable.
examiner_focus: A new question which very few candidates attempted, and those that did totally missed the point. The question specifically asks for an engine COOLING WATER waste heat recovery system, but candidates who attempted it described a waste heat STEAM system instead. The trap word is "cooling water": jacket water at only ~80–90°C is too low-grade to boil water into useful steam, so the electricity-generating cycle must use an Organic Rankine Cycle with a low-boiling-point organic working fluid, not an exhaust-gas steam turbine.

canonical_answers.title: Report — Turbocharger Failure: Seized Turbine-End Bearing & Shaft Damage, Fleet-Wide Preventive Measures
canonical_answers.answer_markdown:
**As Chief Engineer Officer on a vessel with a single 6-cylinder two-stroke crosshead propulsion engine and two turbochargers, one of which fails (seized turbine-end bearing, damaged shaft, inoperable): report for the Engineering Superintendent detailing the failure and cause, explaining how it happened, fleet-wide preventive procedures, and the steps taken to operate the engine at reduced power (16)**

**1. Introduction**: the affected turbocharger (one of two identical units supplying scavenge air in parallel) failed without prior major alarm — first indication was a sudden rise in exhaust gas temperature on several cylinders, a drop in scavenge air pressure, and unusual noise/vibration from the turbocharger. The turbine end bearing was found seized, with the shaft scored, bent/distorted and possibly fractured, rendering the unit inoperable. Load was reduced immediately to protect the remaining turbocharger and engine.

**2. Cause of the failure and how it happened** — root cause: lubrication failure to the turbine end bearing, leading to overheating, seizure and mechanical destruction of the shaft. Sequence:

1. **Initial lubrication deficiency** — partial or complete loss of LO supply/pressure to the turbine end bearing, possibly from blockage/restriction in the supply line or orifice, failure of the T/C lube oil pump or choked filters, oil contamination (water ingress, fuel dilution, metallic particles), or bearing clearance increased beyond limits from normal wear (allowing excessive oil leakage and starvation under load).
2. **Overheating and seizure** — without adequate oil film, the bearing overheated rapidly under high exhaust gas temperature and rotational speed; the bearing material softened/melted, seizing the shaft journal within the housing.
3. **Shaft damage** — once seized, the continuing drive from exhaust gases caused the shaft to twist, score heavily and suffer mechanical damage (possible bending/cracking), making it impossible to rotate the rotor safely.
4. **Secondary effects** — the sudden loss of one turbocharger caused an immediate drop in scavenge air pressure, leading to richer combustion, rising exhaust temperatures and increased thermal loading on the remaining turbocharger and engine. No prior major vibration or bearing-temperature-trend alarm was recorded, indicating the failure developed rapidly once lubrication was compromised.

**3. Actions taken onboard to operate at reduced power**:

- **Isolation of the damaged turbocharger** — shut down and isolated on both exhaust gas and air sides (where design permits); the rotor secured against rotation to eliminate risk of exhaust gas leakage, vibration transmission, or further mechanical failure.
- **Controlled reduction of engine power** — load gradually reduced, currently operated at approximately 55–65% of MCR (subject to confirmation from Superintendent and Class), because the remaining turbocharger cannot supply sufficient scavenge air for full-load combustion (risking very low air-fuel ratio, incomplete combustion, excessive exhaust temperatures, thermal overload of pistons/exhaust valves/liners); to protect the remaining turbocharger from overspeed/overload; to maintain stable combustion within acceptable exhaust temperature margins; and to comply with the engine builder's emergency operating instructions for single-turbocharger operation.
- **Enhanced monitoring and control** — continuous monitoring of all cylinder exhaust temperatures (kept as balanced as possible), scavenge air pressure, remaining turbocharger speed/vibration/bearing temperatures; fuel rack position limited manually or via the load limiter; increased frequency of scavenge space inspections; auxiliary systems (cooling water, lube oil) operated with extra margins; Bridge informed and speed adjusted for safe navigation.

**4. Recommendations for fleet-wide preventive measures**:

1. **Turbocharger bearing inspection and replacement policy** — strict adherence to OEM-recommended running hours (typically 20,000–30,000 hours or earlier based on condition); mandatory boroscopic inspection of turbine and compressor ends at every major overhaul or on any abnormal symptom.
2. **Lubricating oil management** — enhanced LO analysis programme for turbocharger systems (particle count, water content, viscosity, metal content); regular cleaning/replacement of T/C lube oil filters and strainers; verification of correct oil type and pressure at the T/C inlet under all load conditions.
3. **Condition monitoring upgrade** — continuous vibration monitoring/trending on all turbochargers; bearing temperature sensors with trending and pre-alarm settings (not just high-high shutdown); regular review of exhaust gas temperature spreads and scavenge pressure trends as early indicators.
4. **PMS review** — update turbocharger PMS jobs to include more frequent checks of oil supply lines, orifices and drains; include "turbocharger distress" troubleshooting in the Chief Engineer's standing orders.
5. **Training and awareness** — fleet-wide training on early detection of turbocharger problems (noise, vibration, oil consumption, temperature rise); ensure all engineers are familiar with single-turbocharger emergency operation procedures for each engine type in the fleet.
6. **Spares and emergency preparedness** — review stock levels of critical turbocharger spares (bearings, shaft seals, etc.) across the fleet; consider carrying one complete spare turbocharger or major rotating assembly for vessels with critical single-engine propulsion.

**5. Conclusion**: the failure was caused by lubrication starvation leading to bearing seizure and shaft damage. Prompt action allowed the engine to be safely operated at reduced power on the remaining turbocharger, preventing more serious damage to the main engine.
